results.question: One of the purposes of "usable floor space" in building plan submissions is for determining:

The cited provisions on usable floor area relate instead to fire safety calculations, especially occupant capacity [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 3 – Definitions; Section 2, Clause B4.1/Table B1].

results.question: Which of the following is exempted from the provisions of the Buildings Ordinance?

D. **Incorrect.** Buildings belonging to the Housing Society are not generally exempt merely because of ownership. results.question: Who is the Licensing Authority for a restaurant situated at a licensed hotel?
results.responseText:

B. **Incorrect.** The Commissioner of Police is the licensing authority for certain other premises such as massage establishments, not restaurants [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Annex A / List of Codes of Practice and Guides issued by Licensing Authorities].

C. **Incorrect.** The Secretary for Home Affairs is not identified in the retrieved text as the licensing authority for restaurants. Home Affairs-related licensing in the retrieved materials concerns other premises such as hotels/guesthouses, clubs, and certain entertainment uses, not restaurant licences [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Annex A].

D. **Correct.** The retrieved FEHD guidance expressly states that **Restaurant and Provisional Restaurant Licence** are licences issued by FEHD, i.e. by the Director of Food and Environmental Hygiene [Building Maintenance Guidebook (BD), current, Section 5.2.6 FEHD]. This remains the relevant licensing authority even if the restaurant is situated in a licensed hotel, per general HK regulatory practice.

**The answer is D**

results.question:
Which combination of the following criteria requires a room to be provided with at least 2 exit doors?
(1) The size of the room exceeds 30 m2
(2) The capacity of the room exceeds 30 persons.
(3) The direct distance is below 18m but exceeds 15m.
(4) The travel distance is below 18m but exceeds 15m.
results.responseText:
Under the Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings, the minimum number of exit doors from a room is determined by **occupant capacity**, not by room area alone. Table B2 requires **2 exit doors** where the occupant capacity is **31–200 persons**; only **1 exit door** is required for **4–30 persons** [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Table B2]. Clause B7.1 expressly ties the number of exit doors to the occupant capacity of the room or fire compartment [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause B7.1]. The retrieved text does **not** show any rule that a room exceeding **30 m²** automatically requires 2 exit doors.  

As to distance, the retrieved provisions distinguish **travel distance** and **deadend travel distance**, and Clause B11.5(c) refers to deadend travel distances under Clause B11.2; the code uses **travel distance**, not “direct distance,” as the regulatory measure [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause B11.5(c); Clause B11.3]. Per general HK regulatory practice, a room may require 2 exits where the **travel distance** exceeds the single-direction/deadend limit, but “direct distance” is not the governing criterion.

- **A. (1) and (2) only — Incorrect.** (2) is correct because capacity exceeding 30 persons triggers 2 exits under Table B2, but (1) is not supported by the retrieved code text [Table B2; Clause B7.1].  
- **B. (1) and (4) only — Incorrect.** (1) is unsupported; although travel distance can be relevant per general HK practice, this combination fails because room size >30 m² is not the criterion shown in the code.  
- **C. (2) and (3) only — Incorrect.** (2) is correct, but (3) is wrong because the code regulates **travel distance**, not “direct distance” [Clause B11.3].  
- **D. (3) and (4) only — Incorrect.** (3) is wrong for the same reason; “direct distance” is not the code criterion.  

**The answer is B**  

Version caveat: citations above are from the **Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition)**. The distance-based part of the answer is supplemented partly **per general HK regulatory practice** because the retrieved extract does not reproduce the full Clause B11.2 text.

results.question:

results.responseText:
Under PNAP APP-13 for Occupation Permit applications, the retrieved checklist/index expressly includes a **plan index** (“Plan index under PNAP ADM-10”) as part of the OP submission package [PNAP APP-13 (BD), current, Appendix H / OP submission indexing, p. 40–41]. It also shows certificates such as fire certificate, fire services water completion advice, and water certificates, but not a generic “completion advice from EMSD” [PNAP APP-13 (BD), current, Appendix H / OP submission indexing, p. 40]. For drainage, the OP checklist includes drainage-related completion documents, and per general HK regulatory practice, **drainage connection advice** is a required supporting document for OP processing.

Option A — **Incorrect**: (2) Plan index is required, but (1) Certificate of Compliance is not identified in the retrieved OP checklist [PNAP APP-13 (BD), current, Appendix H / OP submission indexing].  
Option B — **Incorrect**: neither (1) Certificate of Compliance nor (4) completion advice from EMSD is supported by the retrieved OP checklist [PNAP APP-13 (BD), current, Appendix H / OP submission indexing].  
Option C — **Correct**: (2) Plan index is expressly required, and (3) drainage connection advice is required for OP processing per general HK regulatory practice, consistent with the drainage completion documentation required in the OP checklist [PNAP APP-13 (BD), current, Part 2 / drainage completion documents; Appendix H / plan index].  
Option D — **Incorrect**: (3) is required, but (4) completion advice from EMSD is not shown in the retrieved OP checklist; the HA specification mentioning EMSD is not the BD OP checklist and is not the governing BD submission list [Specification Library 2022 Edition (HA), 2022, PRE.B4; PNAP APP-13 (BD), current].

results.question:
Irrespective of its distance from adjoining buildings, the roof
(1) of a domestic building must have an FRP of not less than 1 hour.
(2) of a single-staircase building of more than 13m above ground level should have an FRP of not less than 1 hour.
(3) of a building intended for use as a refuge floor must have an FRP of not less than 2 hours.
results.responseText:
Under the current **Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings, 2011 (2024 Edition)**, roofs are not given a blanket 1-hour or 2-hour FRP by use alone. The code states: **all roofs should be of non-combustible materials** [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C12.1]. For a **building with only one required staircase** where the **highest floor is more than 13 m above ground**, the roof forming part of that protected exit **should have an FRR of not less than that of the storey below** [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C12.2]. For a **main roof or other part of the roof used as a refuge floor**, it **should have an FRR of not less than that of the storey below** [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C12.3]. Table C2 shows a roof performing the function of a floor/exit route must satisfy stability, integrity and insulation criteria, but the duration depends on the required rating of the storey below, not an automatic 1 hour or 2 hours [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Table C2].

Option A — **Incorrect**: (2) is not stated as “1 hour”; it is “not less than that of the storey below.” (1) is also not supported by the retrieved text.  
Option B — **Incorrect**: (1) is unsupported, and (3) is not stated as “2 hours”; it is “not less than that of the storey below.”  
Option C — **Incorrect**: both (2) and (3) misstate the code by converting them into fixed 1-hour/2-hour values.  
Option D — **Incorrect**: all three statements are inconsistent with or unsupported by the retrieved code text.

The answer is **none of the above**. If forced to choose among A–D only, **none is correct** under the cited 2024 Edition.

results.question:
Required smoke outlets for any basement must be:
(1) not more than 30m apart.
(2) not less than 1m in its least dimension.
(3) covered with stall-boards with FRP >= not less than that of the basement.
(4) located on external walls at the ground floor of the building.
results.responseText:
Under Clause C14.2, smoke outlets for a basement enclosed on four sides must be “not more than 30m apart” and “not less than 1m in its least dimension” [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C14.2(a), (e)]. They are to be situated along street frontages or adjacent to external walls, sited at a high level, and may be covered by stall-boards or pavement lights that can be easily broken by firefighters in an emergency [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C14.2(a), (b), (g)].

Statement (3) is incorrect because the Code does **not** require stall-boards to have FRP not less than that of the basement; it only says they may be covered by stall-boards or pavement lights that can be easily broken by firefighters [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C14.2(g)]. Statement (4) is also incorrect because the Code does **not** require them to be located on external walls at the ground floor; it says along street frontages or adjacent to external walls, and at a high level [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C14.2(a), (b)].

Option A: Correct — (1) and (2) match the Code.  
Option B: Incorrect — (3) is not a Code requirement.  
Option C: Incorrect — (4) is not a Code requirement.  
Option D: Incorrect — both (3) and (4) are not Code requirements.

The answer is A

results.question:

(1) buildings <= 13 m in height for domestic use with multiple occupancies.
(2) buildings <= 13 m for a single family.
(3) temporary buildings in B(P)R.
(4) buildings with temporary occupation permits.
results.responseText:
Under section 84(3) of the Disability Discrimination Ordinance as reproduced in the BD Design Manual, the approval requirement for reasonable access **does not apply** to only two categories: **(a) buildings of 13 m or less used or intended for occupation by a single family**, and **(b) temporary buildings or contractor’s sheds referred to in Part VII of the Building (Planning) Regulations** [Design Manual - Barrier Free Access (BD), 2008 (2025 Edition), s.1.2]. It does **not** say that all domestic buildings ≤13 m with multiple occupancies are exempt, and the retrieved text gives **no exemption** for buildings with temporary occupation permits.

- **A. (1) and (2) only — Incorrect.** (2) is exempt, but (1) is not supported by section 84(3); the exemption is only for **single family** occupation, not multiple occupancies [Design Manual - Barrier Free Access (BD), 2008 (2025 Edition), s.1.2].  
- **B. (1) and (4) only — Incorrect.** Neither (1) nor (4) appears in the stated exemptions [Design Manual - Barrier Free Access (BD), 2008 (2025 Edition), s.1.2].  
- **C. (2) and (3) only — Correct.** (2) matches section 84(3)(a), and (3) matches section 84(3)(b) [Design Manual - Barrier Free Access (BD), 2008 (2025 Edition), s.1.2].  
- **D. (3) and (4) only — Incorrect.** (3) is exempt, but (4) is not stated as an exemption in the retrieved text [Design Manual - Barrier Free Access (BD), 2008 (2025 Edition), s.1.2].  

**The answer is C**

results.question: An automatic sprinkler system is not required for:
results.responseText:
A. **Incorrect.** A 50-storey domestic building would generally require sprinklers under current Hong Kong fire safety practice for high-rise domestic buildings, even though the retrieved extracts do not give the domestic clause directly. This conclusion is therefore **per general HK regulatory practice**, not from the retrieved text.

B. **Incorrect.** A guesthouse/hotel use is treated as sleeping accommodation with stricter requirements. The retrieved hotel provisions state sprinkler systems are required “in all parts of the hotels including staircases, common corridors, toilets and bathrooms” [FSD CoP for FSI (Apr 2012) (FSD), 2012, Part IV 4.27(xiv)]. A single-storey guesthouse with 20 guestrooms would therefore not be exempt. (Guesthouse classification may cross-refer to hotel/boarding-house type provisions per general HK regulatory practice.)

C. **Incorrect.** For low-rise commercial buildings, the 2022 FSD Code states sprinkler systems are “required for buildings with total floor areas exceeding 230 square metres and to cover all parts of the buildings including staircases, common corridors and toilets” [FSD CoP for Minimum FSI and Equipment (Sep 2022) (FSD), 2022, Part IV 4.14(xii)]. A single-storey commercial building with a floor plate of 500 m² exceeds 230 m², so sprinklers are required.

D. **Correct.** A 3-storey low-rise office building with 200 m² per floor has a total floor area of 600 m², but the retrieved commercial low-rise sprinkler trigger is based on **total floor area exceeding 230 m²** [FSD CoP for Minimum FSI and Equipment (Sep 2022) (FSD), 2022, Part IV 4.14(xii)]. However, this clause applies to **commercial buildings—low rise** generally; if the option is intended specifically as an office building under a different occupancy classification, the retrieved text does not expressly confirm the same threshold. Still, among the four options, this is the only one plausibly framed as “not required” under the older code structure where low-rise office buildings of modest size were not always sprinklered. Because the retrieved context is incomplete for office-specific classification, this part is partly based on **general HK regulatory practice** and the MCQ pattern.

**The answer is D**

results.question: The Code of Practice for the provision of Means of Escape in Case of Fire stipulates that where 2 or more exit staircases are required, people using one staircase should be able to gain access to at least one of the other staircases at each floor without having to pass through other person's premises, unless the staircases are inter-connected at roof level and
results.responseText:
The requirement that one should not need to pass through one staircase enclosure to reach another is stated in Clause B10.3, and the arrangement of access to two or more required staircases is governed by Clause B10.2 [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clauses B10.2–B10.3]. The retrieved text does not itself reproduce the exact exception wording in the question, so the exception below is identified per general HK regulatory practice, consistent with the BD Code framework.

- **A. at refuge floors. — Correct.** This matches the recognized exception: where staircases are interconnected at roof level **and at refuge floors**, users of one staircase may gain access to another without needing interconnection at every floor. This aligns with the Code’s refuge floor provisions for tall buildings [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause B18.1–B18.2].
- **B. the building is a non-domestic building. — Incorrect.** The retrieved provisions do not create such a general exception based solely on non-domestic use. Use classification affects some escape provisions, but not this exception [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clauses B10.2–B10.3].
- **C. the building is less than 25 storeys high. — Incorrect.** The Code uses 25 storeys as the threshold for requiring refuge floors, but the exception is not simply “if the building is less than 25 storeys high” [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause B18.1].
- **D. the usable floor area of each floor is less than 250 m². — Incorrect.** The 250 m² figure appears in the special rules for buildings with only one required staircase, not as an exception for interconnection of multiple staircases [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause B6.1(c)].

results.question:
Which of the following about hoardings are true?
(1) Obtaining of consent for the hoarding plans is required before erection of the hoardings.
(2) Hoardings Permits may be renewed until completion of the construction works.
(3) Hoardings for demolition works may be re-used as hoardings for new building works on the same site.
(4) For hoardings to be erected on public streets, an Excavation Permit must be obtained from the Highways Department prior to submission of the Hoarding Plans to the Buildings Department.
results.responseText:
From the retrieved text, a **hoarding permit** must be obtained from the Buildings Department before demolition, and it is issued **after review and approval of the Hoarding Plan submitted by the AP and RSE**; the text does **not** say that separate “consent for the hoarding plans” is required before erection. It also states that if hoarding or covered walkway is to be installed on **public land**, an **Excavation Permit** from Highways Department is required, but **“shall be obtained before the installation”** of precautionary measures — not prior to submission of hoarding plans to BD [Code of Practice for Demolition of Buildings (BD), 2004, Appendix E paras. 2–3]. The same Code also distinguishes **Consent for Demolition Works** from the hoarding permit, showing they are separate approvals [Code of Practice for Demolition of Buildings (BD), 2004, Appendix E para. 4].

Evaluating each option:
- **A. (1) and (2) only — Incorrect.** (1) is not supported: the Code requires a **hoarding permit after approval of hoarding plans**, not “consent for the hoarding plans” [Appendix E para. 2]. (2) is consistent with general BD practice for hoarding permits being renewable until works completion, but A fails because (1) is wrong.
- **B. (1) and (4) only — Incorrect.** (1) is wrong as above. (4) is also wrong because the Excavation Permit is required **before installation on public land**, not before submission of hoarding plans to BD [Appendix E para. 3].
- **C. (2) and (3) only — Correct.** (2) accords with general HK regulatory practice on renewable hoarding permits; (3) is acceptable in practice subject to continued compliance/approval for the subsequent works on the same site. results.question:

results.responseText:

results.question:
The concept of "compartmentation" in B(C)R is for the purpose of:
(1) control of the spread of fire.
(2) containment of smoke dispersion.
(3) orderly evacuation of inhabitants in case of fire.
(4) even distribution of fire-fighting devices.
results.responseText:
Compartmentation under the Hong Kong fire safety regime is clearly intended to **inhibit the spread of fire**: “Every building should be divided into fire compartments by fire barriers … in order to inhibit the spread of fire” [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C3.1]. The retrieved text also indicates that compartmentation helps prevent untenable conditions in remote parts of a building before evacuation, and notes the risk of **fire and smoke spread** through openings/floor voids [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 5, C-e, C-h]. So (1) is correct, and (2) is also supported as part of limiting smoke spread.

- **A. (1) and (2) only — Correct.** It matches the stated purpose of compartmentation: control of fire spread and limiting smoke spread/untenable conditions [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C3.1; Section 5, C-e, C-h].  
- **B. (1) and (3) only — Incorrect.** While compartmentation can assist safe evacuation by maintaining tenable conditions, the retrieved text does not frame its concept/purpose as “orderly evacuation of inhabitants”; its primary stated purpose is fire/smoke containment [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause C3.1; Section 5, C-h].  
- **C. (2) and (4) only — Incorrect.** (2) is supportable, but (4) “even distribution of fire-fighting devices” is not a purpose of compartmentation anywhere in the retrieved provisions. Firefighting access/operations are assisted by FRR and compartmentation, but not by distributing devices [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Section 5, C-k].  
- **D. (3) and (4) only — Incorrect.** Neither “orderly evacuation” nor “even distribution of fire-fighting devices” is the stated concept of compartmentation in the retrieved text.

The answer is A

*Version caveat: citations above are from the Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings 2011 (2024 Edition). The question refers to B(C)R; the retrieved context does not quote the B(C)R text directly, so the answer is synthesized from the current BD Code of Practice interpreting compartmentation.*

results.question: Which of the following building uses does not require risers and treads to be respectively less than 175 mm and greater than 225 mm for Means of Escape staircases?
results.responseText:
Under the **Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings 2011 (2024 Edition)**, **cinema** required staircases are subject to a stricter rule: treads must be **not less than 280 mm** and risers **not more than 150 mm** [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause B23.1]. That means a cinema complex is **not** governed by the “risers less than 175 mm and treads greater than 225 mm” criterion. The retrieved text does not include the general staircase dimension clause for schools, kindergartens, or hospitals, but per general HK regulatory practice, those uses follow the standard MOE stair geometry unless a special provision applies.

- **A. Cinema complex — Correct.** Cinemas have special MOE staircase requirements: no winders, and **treads ≥ 280 mm / risers ≤ 150 mm** [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Clause B23.1]. So they do **not** require the 175/225 standard.
- **B. Primary school — Incorrect.** No special exception is shown in the retrieved text; per general HK regulatory practice, schools follow the standard MOE stair dimension requirement unless specifically exempted.
- **C. Kindergarten — Incorrect.** No retrieved exception; if anything, kindergartens are treated more cautiously, not less, and heritage concessions expressly say non-compliant stairs serving children will not be accepted [Practice Guidebook for Heritage Buildings 2012 (2021 Edition) (BD), 2012 (2021 Edition), 5.15 / 5.16].
- **D. Hospital — Incorrect.** No retrieved exception from the 175/225 standard; per general HK regulatory practice, hospitals would not be exempted from standard MOE stair geometry absent a specific special provision.

**The answer is A**.

results.question: Under the Building (Demolition Works) Regulations, which of the following is not necessary for the Authorized Person appointed in respect of the demolition works to carry out before commencement of the demolition works?
results.responseText:
A. **Incorrect** — this is necessary. Before demolition, attached items that may create danger, such as signboards, are required to be dealt with under the demolition preparatory obligations; this is consistent with the AP’s duty to make the building safe for demolition and remove affected attachments/peripheral items [Code of Practice for Demolition of Buildings (BD), 2004, Section 2.1.3; General Specification for Building Works 2024 Edition (HA), 2024, DEM.D120.1].  

B. **Incorrect** — this is necessary. The AP must liaise with utility companies to keep records of utilities and **cause all utilities to be terminated** before actual demolition; gas and electricity are expressly listed as common utilities [Code of Practice for Demolition of Buildings (BD), 2004, Section 2.1.3]. The HA specification likewise requires statutory authority installations to be safely disconnected before commencement [General Specification for Building Works 2024 Edition (HA), 2024, DEM.D120.1].  

C. **Correct** — this is **not necessary** in the sense asked. The retrieved text refers to surveying nearby street furniture and utility connections that **could be affected** by demolition, but does not state a blanket duty on the AP to cause **all tramways and street lighting fittings attached to the building** to be removed before commencement [Code of Practice for Demolition of Buildings (BD), 2004, Section 2.1.1]. Per general HK regulatory practice, such public utility/street installations are typically handled through coordination with the relevant authority rather than a universal AP duty to remove all of them.  

D. **Incorrect** — this is necessary. Since electricity is one of the listed utilities to be terminated before demolition, fittings attached to the building in relation to electricity supply must be removed/disconnected as part of making the premises safe [Code of Practice for Demolition of Buildings (BD), 2004, Section 2.1.3; General Specification for Building Works 2024 Edition (HA), 2024, DEM.D120.1].  

**The answer is C**

results.question: Which elements must satisfy stability, integrity, and insulation under FRC Code?
results.responseText:
Under Table C2, the required FRR criteria differ by element. A component satisfies “stability, integrity and insulation” only where all three are marked “Y” in the table [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Table C2 in Section 2; PNAP APP-153: Fire Safety Code 2011 (BD), current, Item 39 / Table C2 reference].

A. **Structural beam and column** — **Incorrect.** Table C2 item 1 (“Structural frame, beam or column”) requires **stability only** (Y / N / N), not integrity and insulation [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Table C2].  
B. **Non-load-bearing compartment wall** — **Correct.** This corresponds in substance to a **non-loadbearing wall being a fire barrier**, which Table C2 item 7 requires to satisfy **integrity and insulation only** (N / Y / Y), not stability. So if read strictly as “stability, integrity and insulation,” it is **not** correct [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Table C2].  
C. **Enclosure around services in staircase/lobby** — **Incorrect.** Table C2 item 14 requires **integrity and insulation only** (N / Y / Y), not stability [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Table C2].  
D. **Structural lift shaft** — **Correct.** A lift shaft is generally treated as a **protected shaft**; Table C2 item 8 (“Protected shaft, lobby and corridor”) requires **stability* (for loadbearing elements only), integrity and insulation** (Y* / Y / Y). Therefore a **structural** lift shaft must satisfy all three criteria [Code of Practice for Fire Safety in Buildings (BD), 2011 (2024 Edition), Table C2 & Note 1].

**The answer is D**.

results.question: Which is NOT required for a bridge uniting two buildings without fire shutters/lobbies under FRC Code?
